The house resumed from Thursday, March 17, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.

Mr. Speaker, to any keen observer of politics it is apparent that the government is not on "easy street" to-day. It does not like the turn that this debate has taken, and hon. members opposite who have spoken in support of the resolution have tried to introduce political issues entirely apart from the subject matter and thus to becloud the real issue before the house. This is done in an endeavour to have- the country forget the two main points of this resolution, to wit, relief for farmers and the unemployed, and the constitutional aspect -of the powers sought by the government to carry out this relief.
By some hon. gentlemen on your right, Mr Speaker, we have been accused of playing politics, and we have been severely criticized for the course we took during the by-election in Three Rivers-St. Maurice, and throughout the late provincial election in Quebec. The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) was severely taken to task by the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) for some of his utterances during the campaign in Three Rivers-St. Maurice. The hon. member for

Unemployment Continuance Act
Dorchester attempted to make political capital out of the result of that by-election. Apparently to please his political chief, he told the house that the result of that byelection represented the unanimous opinion of the province of Quebec in favour of the Tory party. That is far from the fact. The hon. gentleman forgot to state that another byelection took place about the same time in the riding of East Hamilton in this province, always regarded as a safe Conservative seat, but the government candidate was overwhelmingly defeated, and to-day East Hamilton is represented in this house by a Labour member. The hon. member for Dorchester also told the house that the people of Quebec, and more especially the younger generation, were enthusiastic in their admiration of the right hon. leader of the Conservative party, that in fact he was the idol of the province. Many counties in my province, including the county which I have the honour to represent in this house, gave very large majorities to the supporters of the Liberal party at the election in 1930, and I affirm to the house and to the country that the majority of the electors of Quebec as well as the younger generation are not at all enthusiastic admirers of the right hon. leader of the government. Our young men do not regard him as their idol and they decline to follow him. Speaking for my own county, I am confident that our people both old and young are ardent supporters of the right hon. leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Mackenzie King) and our leader in Quebec, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe).
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that those hon. gentlemen who have followed the lead of the hon. member for Dorchester do not represent the real feeling of the people of my province. Those hon. members, it is true, were returned to this house at the election of 1930, but at the last provincial election they were not able to return any of their candidates for the local house. Last August the province of Quebec in the most unmistakable terms returned a verdict of confidence in the Liberal administration which has been controlling the affairs of the province for the last thirty-four years. On that occasion the electors of Quebec had a chance to choose between the Hon. Mr. Tasehereau and Mr. Houde, and by an overwhelming majority they showed their preference for the leader of the administration that had enjoyed the confidence of the province for the past thirty-four years rather than turn to a demagogue like the provincial leader of the Tory party. Let me remind hon. gentlemen to your right, and more especially the

hon. member for Dorchester, that although they may try to belittle our leader in Quebec, my hon. friend from Quebec East, they are playing a very poor game, and they may rest assured that long after they have gone into the valley of oblivion the name of the Hon. Ernest Lapointe will be held in honour and esteem by many generations yet unborn, for he will stand in history as one of the greatest men of our race both in the province of Quebec and in the dominion.
It is not surprising, Mr. Speaker, to hear our hon. friends opposite talking in such a reckless fashion. They were over-enthusiastic after the general election of 1930, and they thought they could repeat their success by fooling the people again in 1931 at the provincial election, but the electors of my province were wiser then than they were in 1930. Our friends opposite are bad losers, and having suffered a severe defeat in the provincial election, naturally they vent their disappointment upon our esteemed leader in Quebec, my hon. friend from Quebec East. At the next federal election I am convinced that the electors of Quebec will display the same sound judgment as they did at the recent provincial election, and that their example will be followed by the electors of the other provinces, and they will send back to their homes our friends opposite so that they may have an opportunity to meditate over their defeat.
We have been accused by some members on your right, Mr. Speaker, of unduly delaying the adoption of this resolution, and thereby becoming responsible for the suffering of the unemployed because this measure of relief is not enacted immediately. But the blame is not to be laid at our door; rather it is the fault of the government which waited for over a month after the opening of the session before introducing this resolution. On reference to the orders of the day it will be found that it was only after the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) had introduced his amendment on the motion to go into supply that the government decided to bring this resolution before the house. The debate has not been unduly long; to-day we are entering on the eighth day. I take issue with the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) who stated the other day that the debate had been in progress for over two weeks. Only thirty-seven members of the official opposition have spoken so far, and they have been joined in debate by fifteen of our hon. friends on the opposite side and by seven members representing various groups on this side of the house-fifty-nine all told.

Unemployment Continuance Act
In 1926 it will be- recalled that there were debates continuing for weeks and weeks, and in 1930 also, when this very question of unemployment was an issue the majority of hon. gentlemen who were then sitting on this side got up one after another and read to the house carefully prepared briefs that had been drafted for them by their party organization. Are there two kinds of justice, one for the Tories and one for the Liberals? If in the days of 1926 and- in 1930 it was right to appose the resolutions and motions proposed by the government of the day, Mr. Speaker, surely to-day we should be given the same freedom of speech and the same liberty of action enjoyed by the Tory party in those days: After all we are here to perform a duty. When we took our places in this house we took an oath of office, and we cannot let this resolution pass, after hearing speeches such as those delivered by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Railways and Canals, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, without entering our protest. I should like to refer especially to the speech delivered in this house the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), in which he said:
It is true that at that time an appropriation might have been voted, and it was very largely the burden of the complaint of some hon. members that that was not done, but I invite hon. gentlemen to consider this, that when an appropriation is passed the purpose for which it is to be used must be specified, and the Auditor General and other officers of the crown in scrutinizing expenditures under such an appropriation, always keep the government very closely to the purpose specified in such a vote.
That is the reason, Mr. Speaker, why the government to-day ccmes before this house asking permission to evade that scrutiny of every appropriation voted by parliament which is required by the laws of our country. It is our prerogative to see where our money goes, the money which comes from the taxpayers of this country, and to see that the government does not commit any abuses in the use of that money. That is the reason why this debate is going on. Further, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
We have certain commitments which have been made under the act; that is, agreements have been entered into with each of the provinces and various works of a different character are being carried on by the provinces with the aid of the dominion, and we ask for an extension of the act for two months, because the difficulties which then confronted the country have not been surmounted. . . .
If it were only to carry out such commitments and finish such works as have been undertaken under this act, speaking for myself and I think for all hon. members on this side of the house, there would be no objection to letting the bill pass, because it would be simply completing those works which have been undertaken for the benefit of the people. But the Minister of Trade and Commerce also said that further relief was required, and that is the point upon which we take issue. While parliament is sitting, and while we are here to decide these issues as representatives of the people, we do not want these powers given to the government. We are here to vote upon any amount of money required by this government to carry on its relief woi'k in the cities and throughout the country.
Since the government has been in power I think it is safe to say that it has been given by the country at large and by the opposition in this house fair play, a free hand and ample opportunity to inaugurate any policies it desired to bring into force; it has not been hampered unduly by the opposition. But discussion is necessary on the part of any opposition, though that is net synonymous with inaction or acquiescence. We are not here simply to listen to the government and abide by its dictates; we are not supposed to say "ditto" to everything the government may propose. The country expects that at all times the opposition shall be vigilant in the preservation of established rights and the liberties of the people, and do all in its power to prevent the usurpation of any rights or powers which do not belong to those entrusted with the government of the country. It is the duty of the opposition to stand by its own principles and policies, especially when there exists throughout the country to an appreciable extent a critical attitude towards the government. It is the duty of the opposition to express that attitude in this house and to present our criticism with regard to the measures brought forward by the government. In the province from which I come I may say there is a good deal of criticism directed against the government as to the manner in which this unemployment relief money has been administered, and also as to the way the government has put in force the policies it promised to bring forward during the election of 1930. That is why this debate has gone on for some days and the reason why it may go on for some time longer.
I think we are all in agreement with the object of this resolution; that is, we all desire to seek ways and means of relieving the farmers and the unemployed throughout the country. But as to the methods adopted in the past and proposed to be continued in the future we disagree. This proposal is too far
Unemployment Continuance Act

unemployment and farm relief, has had to go to the very source to which, as we pointed out before, it was necessary to go in order to settle the problem. We stated that cooperation was necessary among the municipalities, the provinces and the federal government.
We have been told of the wonderful success that has been achieved in Saskatchewan through the relief commission appointed there under the bill; yet a general relief unemployment commission, such as has been advocated by my leader, has been refused by the government. Notwithstanding the efforts of the government, the situation has been going from bad to worse, and to-day we have only to refer to the speeches of certain western members in order to see that in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta conditions to-day are worse than they have ever been. We find the members from those provinces asking for feed for cattle and for seed for the spring. We have also heard of the complaints that were made in British Columbia regarding the administration of the act. Owing to the maladministration of the act, it has been necessary to appoint a commission to investigate matters. I have in my hand an editorial which appeared in Le Soleil of Quebec on August 27 last. This editorial discloses the fact that certain hon. members who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker, attempted to play politics in the last provincial elections in Quebec. They tried to make use of the efforts put forth by the government to grant unemployment relief in order to force the electors to vote in their favour. This editorial quotes a letter which had been written by the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Fortin) dated August 22, 1931, addressed to the electors of Bienville and Lauzon. The editorial is in French and is as follows:
(Translation):
Sell Yourself Or Starve!
Such seems to have been the motto of certain Houdist electioneers in the last campaign. Sell yourself or starve! These words are actually embodied in certain documents that we have in our possession and which bring shame on those who had them circulated. It is impossible to close our eyes, in connection with this literature, to the blackmail directed against the liberty of citizens.
The following circular letter which Dr. Emile Fortin, member for Levis, at Ottawa, addressed to the electorate of his county to bribe them by promising bread in return for their vote in favour of Mr. Noel Belleau, the Houdist candidate, is an instance of the corruption carried on in this election:
[Mr. Casgrain.l
Do You Want Work?
Levis, August 22, 1931.
Electors of Bienville,
Electors of Lauzon.
Famine Is At Your Door!
There are signs that winter will be severe! Unemployment increases: Workmen of Lauzon, whatever may be your party attachment or feelings, do you want work? Do you want bread? Help me! and put your trust in the only government which can relieve you.
Heretofore, I have not spared my time or energy to help you. Shall you, by an unfavourable and thoughtless vote undo my twelve months of work and anxiety?
You need the Dominion government. Vote for it by voting for Noel Belleau, thus you will be endorsing the following contracts:
Fire-engine boat, $350,000.
Repairs to the Prince Edward Island, $270,000.
Repairs to the dry docks, $36,000.
Repairs to the forts, $150,000.
Repairs to government boats, $100,000.
Repairs at the engineers' camp-target range,

Think how advantageous it would be for Levis if I had to help me: Noel Belleau, K.C., minister of the crown, at Quebec; Hon. Maurice Duprd, a son of Levis, minister at Ottawa; Mr. Onesime Gagnon, member for Dorchester and future minister in the Bennett administration.
What help can Mr. Belanger be to you in contrast with what we can do for you?
The provincial government can do nothing without the support of the government, at Ottawa.
Mr. Bennett can give you prosperity. Three Rivers endorsed his policy and received $700,000.
Let Lauzon and Bienville do their share, they will be given in return work and prosperity.
Workmen of Lauzon if you disown the Conservative party what can you expect from it next winter ?
(Sgd.) Dr. Emdle Fortin,
Member at Ottawa.
Never has the Conservative party admitted more impudently to what means they resort to bribe the people.
"Three Rivers endorsed his policy and received $700,000." What a confession! So, when the country is in the throes of a critical economic crisis, the Conservative party, at Ottawa, in an endeavour to destroy the Liberal party, grant almost three-quarters of a million to the ratepayers in Three Rivers to purchase their votes and ease their conscience! A party which resorts to such means deserves to Be wiped out. It is what the Liberals did, last Monday, to the Houdists, and it is what they will do in four years to Mr. Bennett.
I shall translate a part of this editorial as it may prove interesting to the people at large. The letter says that Bennett alone can give prosperity, that Three Rivers has approved of his policy and has received $700,000 in the form of relief, and the electors of Bienville and Lauzon are advised to do likewise and they will see a return to pros-

Unemployment Continuance Act
perity. They are told that if they renounce the Conservative party they cannot expect to receive anything during next winter.
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. members who sit on your right have not used this act to play politics, I should like to know what they have done. They used it to appeal to the people in the province of Quebec during the last provincial election. Had there been appointed a relief commission, as advocated by my right hon. leader such things would not have occurred. I think I am safe in saying that this act has proved to be inadequate and futile, its administration has been wasteful and extravagant and the necessary relief has not reached the people. The hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) quoted last night an extract from the Financial Post which showed the cost of the administration of this act. The figures showed that the debt of the country has been increased because of the expenses of administration.
Has unemployment been relieved and work given to the people? I have before me figures which show that in September, 1931, one year after the government had taken office, 7,798 firms were employing 972,537 people. In January, 1932, the figures stood at 7,832 firms employing 835,960 people, a considerable decrease in the number employed. In February, 1932, the totals had declined further to 7,766 firms employing 819.175 people. These figures show that not very much work has been provided for the people of Canada. The index of employment in industry in Canada is at its lowest ebb since 1922. Who is responsible for this? The Prime Minister admitted that the government was responsible when he made the speeches to which I have alluded.
The hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) speaking in the house on February 23, 1932, said:
As time went on it was apparent that further measures would have to be adopted in order that those in want might be given such employment as would tide them over, and the result was the legislation of last session. Under that legislation 334,301 persons have been given employment up to January 31. 1932, the total number of man-days being 7,415,973. The total commitments necessary to carry on the work to February 22, 1932, amounted to $76,426,387. the federal government's share being $32,822,847. This work is still proceeding. The figures I have given will be subject to some slight variation when the report is tabled which I trust will be shortly.
The total cost was 876,426,387 to provide 7.415,973 man-days, or slightly more than $10 for every day's work provided. Where did the balance go? Is that the way to take care of unemployment? When the $20,000,000 was voted in 1930 we were given to understand
that many public works would be undertaken in order to provide unemployment relief. After the act had been passed the Minister of Labour wrote to various members of the government and of the opposition asking us to point out the various works which would be necessary in our constituency in order to assist the people. I replied to the hon. minister under date of August 15, 1931. He acknowledged receipt of my letter but he did not take cognizance of the requests which I had made and the suggestions which I had given.
I cannot see how we can abide by the dictates and requests of the government and pass this resolution without protest. We are being asked to extend for two months legislation which vests in the government all the powers which this house has over the control of public money. I have demonstrated the results which have been obtained from the administration of this act and I cannot conceive how we, representing our constituencies and having taken an oath to fulfil our mandates, can give to the government while parliament is sitting the rights granted under the constitution to this house. We are being asked to do away with the committees of supply and ways and means, the very bases of the parliamentary system.
Hon. members of the government have asked for cooperation but how can we cooperate when we do not know what amount will be expended and for what purpose? How can we cooperate with the leader of the government when he does as he pleases, even with his own supporters and refuses to accept counsel or advice from anyone? Most of the hon. members on this side who have spoken, and I think some on the other side, will agree that the gentleman who leads the government to-day wants to do it by himself alone. Hon. members have called him Nero and Mussolini, and the names of other absolute dictators in history. We have also called him Mussolini. For my part, last year I said what I thought of him and I do not want to say any more, because the people of the country know him well enough.
I protest against this resolution, and this is the reason I and other members have been carrying on this debate. We contend that if this resolution is passed, it means that we shall be giving up all the rights and privileges for which our forefathers fought in 1837 and for which a fight was carried on in England hundreds of years ago, in order that the representatives of the people might obtain control of the public money.
Hear, hear.

The
Prime Minister should remember that this is no time for rash action, that this is no time for him to test the extent of his power, for "they who sow the wind shall reap the whirlwind." Instead of encroaching upon our government system and of introducing reckless measures, the Prime Minister should endeavour, in these hard times, to proceed along regular lines and abstain from any novel departure likely to unduly magnify, in the public mind, the seriousness of the situation. Such was, during the war, the policy followed by statesmen who were well worth the present Prime Minister, and as was already pointed out, by this resolution, the Prime Minister is attempting to assume power a hundredfold larger than those enjoyed by Sir Robert Borden under the War Measures Act and the War Appropriation Act.
The Prime Minister should not, also, be unmindful of the lessons of history. One cannot, with impunity, offend public feeling, nor can one hurt with impunit>T that sense of justice and freedom so deeply rooted in the hearts of every Canadian. One cannot, with impunity, ignore the system of government we owe to the wisdom of our ancestors nor could one demolish such barriers as the people have seen fit to erect against the tendency to absolutism on the part of the executive. The Prime Minister should recollect that the movement which took place a hundred years ago in connection with the control of public expenditures by the peoples' representatives led to the rebellion of 1837-1838. And in support of this, I may cite the very words of Lord Gosford, governor general of Lower Canada in 1837, and therefore in a better position than anyone else to know the situation. In the debate that took place in the House of Lords on the union of the two Canadas, Lord Gosford stated that the chief responsibility for the rebellion was to be laid at the door of those who having, at the conquest,

Unemployment Continuance Act
monopolized all the money, all the power and all the important posts, persisted in governing the Canadians without their consent and participation. The following is an extract of the statement of Lord Gosford, as found in the history of Canada:
There are, specially in Montreal and in the vicinity, a number of English speaking citizens to whom every liberal-minded and independent man must be hostile, whose acts and behaviour have been characterized by a spirit of domination over the whole population of French origin; they have continuously aimed at acquiring power and exercising patronage in the country. They are the men who must be held chiefly responsible for the troubles that have recently occurred.
I earnestly urge upon the Prime Minister of Canada to ponder over the events that took place previous to the rebellion of 1837, and to seriously consider the statement of Lord Gosford, former governor general of Lower Canada.
We are told, Mr. Speaker, that this measure must be passed in the shortest possible time, it being a matter of life and death for the unemployed and the farmers, and that any opposition to it means a delay in granting relief. I take the strongest exception to a threat of that sort, to that intimidation and duplicity to which recourse has been had so frequently during the last two years in connection with unemployment. It has been said, on this side of the house, that the government had organized the unemployed into a regular profession; more than that, they have used unemployment as a pretext and a justification for all their misdeeds. Every time the government wishes to camouflage any of their arbitrary acts, every time they want to work in the dark and frame some plot against our parliamentary institutions, they plead the same old excuse, the same old motive, that is the necessity of giving relief to the unemployed, to the farmers, and of rendering assistance to the needy in this country. I protest against that procedure on the part of the government and against such an exploitation of public distress, which is simply used to play politics.
It is needless to repeat, in the course of this debate, the offer so many times made by us to the Prime Minister to the effect that we are willing to vote any amount of money. We have offered, and still offer to him to vote supplies, provided he can give sufficient cause therefor. We are entitled to know from him the reason for the expenditures to be incurred by the government. We would feel remiss to our duty and, for my part, I would feel unworthy of the mandate I hold from my electors, should I not raise my voice against 41761-79i
that mode of procedure on the part of the government and should I not, after the other hon. members who spoke before me, insist upon the government for a statement of their reasons and motives for the contemplated expenditures.
We have heard our hon. friends on the government side, the butter-makers of 1930, not to say the "buttery" promise makers of 1930, speak in laudatory, but senseless and ludicrous terms, of the Prime Minister and of "Bennettism." Instead of wasting such a torrent of praise, our friends, specially the government followers in the province of Quebec group, should have called upon the government to take action. I do not say that they should have appealed to the liberality of government, as they were in duty bound to do, but it would have been better for them to secure the aid of the government in behalf of the farming community of Eastern Canada, particularly of the province of Quebec represented by us in this house. I charge the government with having completely failed to do anything for the relief of agriculture in Quebec. The farmers in that province may not lament as loudly as those in some other parts of the country,-they are not in the habit of taking such political action,-but the fact remains that they keenly feel the hardships of the present depression, which has been made worse through the folly of high protection. If it be in order to give relief to other classes of the community, if it be fair to erect exceedingly high tariff walls for the protection of the manufacturing interests, for instance, it is equally fair and proper to afford the same measure of protection to agriculture.
The legislation we are now asked to revive is entitled: "The Unemployment and Farm Relief Act". I fear no contradiction when I say that the farmers in the province of Quebec have benefited in no way from the legislation we are asked to extend. Should it be revived, I am quite sure that it would not be more beneficial to the farming class in Quebec than afforded them the old act that expired on the first of March last.
Instead of entitling the act: "The Unemployment and Farm Relief Aot" the government should, abstaining themselves from any camouflage and deceit, call it: "An Act for the relief of financiers at bay." In the course of this debate, it has developed that the act; was used to come to the help of the bankers,, insurance companies, financiers and bondholders in certain western provinces, rather than to actually give relief to the unemployed and to the farmers.

Unemployment Continuance Act

(Translation,) For the
relief of cement dealers.

And for the relief of railway ties manufacturers.
If the government had been sincere in its effort to improve the conditions of the farming community, they would have done more than the small works undertaken, and they would have adopted means other than the makeshift measures carried out since the unemployment act is in existence. A few moments ago, I said that no benefits had accrued to the farmers of the province of Quebec from the enforcement of that legislation. I might perhaps qualify this statement to a certain extent, for some works have been attempted in winter time, such as, for instance, the hauling of gravel or other unimportant work in connection with road building. But such works, which are mere incidents, simple make shifts and palliatives, have not altered the conditions. At the most, a dozen of men in a parish, have been enabled to earn $10 or $12 working at these jobs in this time of depression. And yet that money was not earned by those who were in the greatest need, but by farmers in easy circumstances; and the reason why those who needed relief the most were unable to secure it was that, having no homes nor rigs of their own, they wene ineligible to employment in connection with the hauling of gravel or other road work, all of which was undertaken in midwinter for the *purpose of relieving unemployment.
I charge the government with having no comprehensive plan, no definite policy for the relief of unemployment, and particularly of agriculture. We have been criticized for our lack of suggestions to the government. If the government had listened to what has been said in this house last session, and during the special session of 1930, as well as to what has been proclaimed almost everywhere, on' the hustings and in the public press, they would have realized that constructive suggestions have been made to them. For my part,
I would humbly suggest to the. government, -and that, obviously, after many others for *the idea is not mine,-that the best way to bring relief to the farmers of Quebec would be to grant a bounty for the clearing and breaking of the soil, which premium would enable the farmers to live with the income from their holdings. In a section of my constituency, as is also the case in the southern part of Montmagny, Dorchester and LTslet, the farmers' lands are not in a sufficiently advanced state of cultivation to support their owners. Until recently, the farmers in that [Mr. Boulanger. I
district mostly earned their living in the bush; but for a year or two, the lumbering activities have ceased, on account of the depression, and the farmers, no longer able to work in the lumber camps and enjoying but a1 soant income from their farm, are now in' the direst need. Last year, I raised that' *question in the house and I also discussed it both in public and in the press. But up to this time the government have not trouhled themselves about that suggestion and did not draw any plan to carry it into effect. Instead of pledging the credit of this country for the security of the bondholders of the western .provinces, instead of spending enormous sums of money in railroad ties or to increase the strength of the police force, for instance, the government would be well advised to appropriate a certain amount in order to carry through the suggestion I have already made and which I am repeating now after many others. The government should cooperate with the provinces with a view to granting a clearing bonus to farmers whose lands are not sufficiently cleared to keep them alive. With such a bonus a farmer could clear let us say thirty or forty acres of his land, and when a farmer has enough land cleared, then all he has to do is to cultivate it, and he is assured of a livelihood1. That is one permanent means of relieving distress among farmers. It woulld be far better than the contrivances and palliatives hitherto used. That would be a good investment, the capital would not be wasted, it would be effective and' profitable, whereas, up to this time, we have simply thrown money away. The government thus could keep a great many farmers permanently on the land, who otherwise, unless we give them some assistance, will have to leave their farms and go to the cities where they will add to the number of unemployed and those who are a public charge. Some will say: "What is the use of having the farmers rooted in their lands? What is the use of promoting a back to the land movement? What is the use of encouraging former farmers who live in the cities to take to agriculture again, since the prices of farm products are so low and the products so hard to sell?" This is my answer: "Even though farm products are cheap, even though farming is not profitable, at least a man can earn his livelihood more easily on the land than in the cities and towns; a farmer is in a better position than the poor laborer who has no work or the mechanic who is unemployed. The latter have to pay for everything they need, even for the water that they drink. In the countryside, they get all that from the soil. The farmer can get enough to eat, he is

Unemployment Continuance Act
sure to have some bread on the shelf and pork in the salting-tub. He is sure of getting vegetables and also wood to warm his house, and that requires but labour on his part. Thus it would intensify the clearing of land and the government would secure a permanent livelihood for a great many .people. By cooperating with the provinces for the granting of a clearing bonus to farmers, that would induce them to cultivate a greater acreage; they would become real farmers thinking only of improving their land and living on what it may yield, and that would keep them awey from the shanties; because, after all, a farmer has nothing to earn by going there. Cultivating the soil is the traditional .mission of our people in the province of Quebec. They are not shantymen, they are not manufacturers, nor mechanics; the only avocation in which they will succeed and for which .they are qualified and competent, is farming.
Mr. Speaker, not only could t'he government cooperate with the provinces for the granting of clearing bonuses in order to expand the land under cultivation, but they could also grant ploughing bonuses for the purpose of inducing the farmers to cultivate more and to improve their lands and thus add to the productive wealth of Canada.
I was speaking a moment ago about the back to the land movement. It is a good way of relieving decidedly and permanently the unemployment situation, and the government ought to foster that movement. The faon. Minister of Immigration (Mr. Gordon) has already commented upon this policy for the return of former farmers to the land, and I congratulate him for it. It is a good move on the part of the government, we give them credit for it, and we appreciate what they have done along these lines. But it is not enough, and the government should intensify that movement and cooperate with the provinces, more especially with the province of Quebec which has done wonderful work in that direction. The province of Quebec has reinstated on the land about five or six thousand families of former farmers who were merely existing or starving in the towns; the government of the province of Quebec helped them to return to their farms where they have become an asset for their country, instead of remaining idle or being a public charge in the cities. Such is the bold suggestion that I am making to the government for the purpose of curing unemployment. I have another suggestion to offer.

I do not think I shall require the whole forty minutes allotted by the rules of the house to express my humble opinion on the merits of the measure that has been submitted to us and which we are now asked to consider and discuss. I need not make a very long speech to enumerate the reasons why we are opposing a measure of this kind, which may lead to the most serious consequences. There is above any other consideration a fundamental principle which we must bear in mind,

Unemployment Continuance Act
that of the legitimate control by the representatives of the people of the revenue derived from taxes imposed upon and paid by the people. In other words, parliament-not the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) or the executive-has the right to appropriate and control all the revenues of the country. That is the fundamental principle which the Prime Minister wishes to forget and to put aside, losing sight of the very important fact that the parliamentary system is in force in this country and that, according to our constitution, the right to appropriate public funds belongs exclusively to parliament. The transfer of powers involved in this resolution simply means a breach and defiance of a fundamental disposition of our constitution.
The government may notice that this resolution has caused a wholesale uprising of fighting energies against this arbitrary measure which is being perpetrated right under a system of constitutional freedom. This is the most arbitrary measure that a government could take in our country. It certainly is a challenge to the liberty which is guaranteed to us by the constitution of this country. Do we not remember the dissensions, the disputes and even the hatreds which the famous question of supply gave rise to. Supply .must be granted freely by the house and to transfer that privilege to the prime minister alone would be equivalent to say that parliament has no reason to exist. To adopt a measure of this kind would simply mean that we are reverting to the unfortunate days of the Family Compact. One recalls how this aristocracy responsible only to the Colonial office in London administered the country's affairs. Land sales, mining operations, customs duties, taxes, in a word, all the country's resources were entrusted to the members of the "Family Compact." Moneys voted for the improvement of roads and highways were expended in other directions. In fact, one could not find out exactly how the money was spent. All these intrigues, all these injustices helped to bring upon us the dark, unhappy days of the rebellion. And it was to prevent for all time a recurrence of such calamities and similar persecutions in the parliamentary arena that our ancestors did not hesitate to fight, shed their blood on the battle-fields or forfeit their lives on the gallows. We can never forget the chapter they wrote.
Now, here is the wording of the resolution the honourable prime minister submits to this house:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of
Canada. 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.
As everybody knows, parliament adopted in the closing days of the 1931 session, at the express request and upon the special representations of the Prime Minister, an extraordinary law the object of which, as represented at the time and as the wording of the law itself made clear, was to confer upon the government special powers relating to unemployment and farm relief as well as the maintenance of peace, order and good government. This is what the draft resolution submitted to parliament stated:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to confer certain powers upon the governor in council in respect to unemployment and farm relief; and for the maintenance of peace, order and good government in all parts of Canada; and to authorize the governor in council to expend for the said purposes out of the consolidated revenue fund such sums as may from time to time be necessary.
The law adopted at that time in accordance with this resolution was to lapse on March 1, 1932. That is what section 8 of the said law enacted and it is this provision the honourable prime minister is now asking this house to amend by extending to May 1st next the time limit of this measure.
The simple recital of these provisions clearly shows this eighteenth day of March, 1932, that this law whose expiry was set for March 1, 1932, has lapsed, is dead and inoperative since several days. As a matter of fact, if in law, certain agreements, for example leases, can in certain cases, imply a continued tenancy' without renewal of lease, the same procedure cannot be applied to a law such as this. Moreover, they are not asking this house to revive the law. Instead, they are asking parliament to modify, alter and amend a law that no longer exists, that lapsed on March 1.
Hear, hear!

Here is
a primary motive which from the standpoint of parliamentary procedure prevents us from considering and much less adopting a measure of this kind that is absolutely ill-grounded. One can invoke many other reasons against its adoption. May I be allowed to point them out as concisely and rapidly as possible, because .many of the speakers who preceded me and whom, by the way, I congratulate upon their excellent speeches, have in the main covered the ground in a very able manner. If I may be allowed, I would like to mention especially the speeches delivered by the right honourable leader of the op-
Unemployment Continuance Act

position (Mr. Mackenzie King), the former Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the hon. member for Labeile (Mr. Bourassa).
It is exceedingly regrettable, indeed, that the right honourable Prime Minister whose talents and industriousness we acknowledge should be intent on wanting to control and administer everything by himself. In so far as this authority relates only to matters of ordinary administration, it is true that we may possibly not have anything to do with such questions, but when things reach a pass where he undertakes, by measures such as those adopted last year and that submitted to us at the present time, to arrogate to himself the absolute and arbitrary control of the expenditure of public moneys, then it is an altogether different matter and constitutes an illegality parliament should not countenance. Such autocracy and such dictatorship have been denounced at sufficient length in the course of the present debate, and one need not dwell further on the subject. However, there is one aspect of this case which reminds me of a gallant English elector who was elected member under very exceptional circumstances. Historians chronicled this very peculiar election case in the following manner. (See Mignault, Parliamentary Law, page 95.)
It is said that an election being held, only one voter, except the sheriff and the returning officer, was present at the nomination meeting. The lone voter took the chair, opened the meeting, called the voters' roll, answered to his own name, and chose himself as member for the constituency. Being the only voter, he was elected by acclamation and the so-called representative of Bute county courageously sat at Westminster.
When we see the right honourable prime minister trying to assume absolute and dictatorial powers such as are conferred by this resolution, we would think that he is ready to revert a few 'Centuries in the past, to go back to that period where such things, as the one I have just mentioned, could occur,
It has been said, and I repeat it, if through such wide powers as are conferred in respect to unemployment and farm relief, and the maintenance of peace, order and good government, the prime minister intends to follow his .past attitude and avails himself of this procuration, this mandate or this authorization to do as he pleases without consulting parliament even when it is in session, our presence here is not needed and it is useless to waste money which could be put to a better use while the country is suffering from hard times, depression and unemployment.
It is to be regretted that the Prime Minister should want to discard the farmali-
TMr. Fontaine.]
ties and procedure which have always been followed by this house so far as voting and spending public funds are concerned. He has taken this irregular course, from the moment of his accession to power, that is during the special session of September, 1930. We all well remember what happened then. The government submitted legislation stipulating that a sum not exceeding twenty million dollars could be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada to relieve unemployment in constructing, extending or improving public works and undertakings, railways, highways, etc., which would assist in providing useful and suitable work for the unemployed. This first step was contrary to the parliamentary procedure always followed in such cases. To obtain this money the gov-vernment should have presented a supply bill first; then they should have painted out clearly what they intended to do with the money; and finally it should have been stipulated that this amount was only available till the end of the fiscal year. The opposition wanted to consider the measure and to raise some objections, even if they concurred in the principle of the bill or in the amount specified, but the right honourable prime minister having stated that if we delayed the adoption of the bill he would be unable to take part in the London conference, this unemployment legislation was immediately passed.
The second false step was taken by this administration towards the end of last session, when the right hon. Prime Minister, for the same reason, that is in respect to unemployment and farm relief, etc., asked parliament to confer on him the wide powers which would enable him to remedy all evils before the next session. It was rather strange that unemployment should still exist at that time, because the right hon. Prime Minister had promised during the election campaign of 1930, that he would put an end to it. We can even say that his party was elected on that definite and formal promise.
The statements made then by the present Prime Minister shall not be soon forgotten. On one occasion after having stressed the fact that there should be no unemployment in a rich country like ours if the government discharged its duties as it should, he added:
The leader of the Liberal party promises consideration of the problem of unemployment, to call a conference to this end, etc., but I promise you to put an end to unemployment or to perish in the attempt.
Later he found out that the crisis could be due to other causes than negligence on the part of the government, and last session in

Unemployment Continuance Act
one of his speeches (Hansard, page 780), he said that speculation brought disaster in its wake, and he added:
It is known that over $400,000,000 of Canadian money was lost last year by speculation in Wall street.
This was almost two years ago. What have been the results? What has happened? Alas, the very opposite of what was expected happened. Not only is the unemployment problem unsolved, but it is getting worse; unemployment is increasing at an alarming rate. And as to fanning; it has never been so completely and entirely stagnant as it is to-day.
And this is the moment chosen by the government to advance another step along the road of irregularity, as I was saying a few moments ago. But if they had some slight excuses to follow that course, in the two first instances, they had no reason whatever to keep on ignoring the constitution and the parliamentary usages and, at the same time, to trifle with the privileges and prerogatives of members of parliament.
Taking this stand and behaving towards parliament as he does, the right hon. Prime Minister surely cannot feel hurt at being designated by such terms as dictator, autocrat, sultan, etc.; or at being compared to Mussolini, Lenin, and to other potentates. Having presented legislation so arbitrary, unfair and radical in character, he should not be surprised if he is given such names. Some of his supporters are shocked on that account, but let them not forget that Liberals will never blame him half as much as did some eminent Conservatives in years gone by. The late Sir Sam Hughes, for example, who was Minister of Defence in a Conservative government, did not hesitate, in 1917, to speak of the present Prime Minister from the floor of this house, in the following terms:
He has brought bad luck to all enterprises, companies and capitalists with whom he has been associated. He is the most striking example of failure in public life which has ever taken place in the Dominion of Canada.
The members of the opposition have said nothing during this debate which at all compares with the preceding paragraph..
The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) pointed out the other day, while speaking on this resolution, that it was very strange to note how lightly the Prime Minister considers our parliamentary traditions to-day, whilst he availed himself of every opportunity, when he was leader of the opposition, to show off as a staunch champion of the British parliamentary traditions, to invoke this or
that precedent to induce members to respect the fundamental basis of our parliamentary institutions. How could such a change come about in this man? We may very well say in this case, "Quantum mutatus ab illo"? But this is not the only instance where he has changed his views or his ideas.
Let us take immigration, for example. On this question as well as on many others, the right honourable Prime Minister is entirely at variance with himself. Last session he stated that the admission of over 100,000 immigrants in this country, in 1929, and during the first seven months of 1930, and the lack of foresight on the part of the last administration, were two of the principal causes of the present depression. On the 21st of April, 1931, at pages 783 and 784 of Hansard, he is reported as follows:
Let us go a step further and examine one of
the great causes of conditions in this country. How many people do hon. members think were brought into Canada from continental Europe, in the year 1929 and seven months of 1930, preceding the time we assumed power? Let me place before the house one statement shown by figures I have in my possession. Do hon. members realize that during that period of time 104,556 people came into this country from central Europe? They came here, and they are now largely being kept by Canadians.
Some hon. Members (Translation):	Hear,
hear.
Mr. Bennett (Translation):	Most of them
are being kept-not all of them-by Canadians, with our taxes. The howl that is heard in some quarters about direct relief arises from the fact that the government of 1929 and the early part of 1930 could not foresee what *was coming. They brought them here in increasing numbers for us to feed.
Moreover the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) stated very recently in this house that this immigration, which took place a little before 1930, was mainly responsible for the unemployment problem. On February 23, at page 440 of Hansard, the hon. minister is quoted as follows:
What was the situation during the months just prior to this government coming into office? I think I am stating what was in the mind of every man who travelled within Canada when I say that the late government, not recognizing the condition that was becoming all too apparent, did not take any steps to curb the undisciplined flow of immigrants into Canada, which had been carried on for three or four years prior to 1930. I want hon. members of the house -to remember this: During the sixteen months ended July 31, 1930, 221,561 people were brought into Canada, 99,367 of whom were adult males. This factor contributed largely to the unemployment problem.
Considering all these statements, it would be of interest to note what were the views at that time of our present Prime Minister, who

Unemployment Continuance Act
was then leader of the opposition, on this question of immigration. Allow me to quote on this subject an extract taken from a speech delivered in this house on February the 11th, 1929:
We have here one of the largest undeveloped areas in the world; we have a very pressing necessity for more people. There need be no misapprehension about that, notwithstanding what has been said from time to time to the contrary. It will be found that the increase of population in this country, brought about through bringing additional people in, will not only lessen unemployment for those who are now in, but will increase all employment.
It seems very strange that when commenting on the speech from the throne, the Prime Minister, then in the opposition, criticized the government for not setting aside sufficient funds to encourage immigration.
There is no need of commenting at length over his words to prove that, at the time, the leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister, worked strenuously to encourage immigration and to show that by such a policy we would decrease unemployment and create new openings for unskilled labour. He was not the only one among the members opposite to propound such a policy. On this same immigration question, the following views were expressed in 1929, by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), at page 2798 of Hansard:
I am not complaining so much of the small number of British immigrants, as of the small number of immigrants, in general. . . . We can receive many times the number of immigrants of all trades that we are to-day receiving.
If our hon. friends opposite have found it possible, within a few years, to change their views and their policy on such an important question, I have no doubt that some day they will realize-when it will 'be perhaps too late -that the measure they have just introduced' is greatly vexatious, arbitrary, unjust, ultra vires and outrages our most cherished parliamentary rights.
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals in his speech on March 9, made an ardent appeal to all the members on your left, sir, requesting their support on the present measure. To answer this invitation, I think it is first necessary to again point out that we are most willing, under the circumstances, to give the government our entire support in helping it to extricate itself from the difficult situation in which it finds itself. The opposition, therefore, has clearly shown and openly stated'-this will be found in all speeches delivered-that we are ready to vote all the money that government may require to meet the situation. All we ask is that the

customary procedure be followed by respecting the privileges and prerogatives of parliament. Otherwise, our presence here is not needed and the holding of this session is unnecessary. To despoil ourselves of these privileges and prerogatives in favour of the Prime Minister and his government would simply mean to be false to 'the mandate we received from those who have asked us to represent them in this house. This we cannot do.
I cannot understand the attitude of hon. members opposite. They know perfectly well, as we do, that one of the fundamental principles of self-government and which has been the cause of so many struggles in this country, so many sacrifices and so many heroic deeds on the part of our forebears^-is that parliament alone possesses, by virtue of the constitution which governs us, the privilege, control and responsibility of the expenditure of public funds. And what is required from us today-by way of cooperation-is to concur, in the midst of a session, without any plausible reason, in a flagrant violation of the constitution. Again I repeat, this we cannot do.
But there is much more. Mention is made of precedents. It is again a minister of the crown, the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) who, in his speech the other day, contended that a precedent had been created by the act passed at the end of last session. I cannot understand how the hon. minister can forget that the main reason given by the Prime Minister to obtain such a blank signature, was precisely that we were on the eve of prorogation and that he absolutely needed such extensive powers to maintain peace, order and good government after parliament had prorogued. I do not see the necessity of further insisting to show clearly that conditions have changed and that such a precedent cannot be invoked, if one wishes to be honest.
However, the argument put forth by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, throws light on the real intentions of the government to resort to so-called precedents which are unfounded, and we have far more cause to very strongly oppose this measure. Since the government intends to authorize itself by such unfounded precedents, it is a further reason to be more watchful and wise and bring to *bear more opposition to such measures and breaches that nothing can justify.
We are not to be deceived nor must we ignore that what is expected from us is nothing else but a blank signature so as to allow the Prime Minister or the cabinet-which after ail is the same thing-to expend the public

Unemployment Continuance Act
funds as they please, no stipulated amount being mentioned. And, they seem astonished even shocked that such an unheard of measure finds opposition and is greatly criticized. But, sir, this year, we have other serious objections to such legislation. One of them, is the use made of this blank signature by the Prime Minister. To facilitate the adoption of this bill, last year, it was stated and guaranteed that its aim was to relieve the unemployed and farmers. How can they explain that, notwithstanding these extraordinary powers and a policy of high protection, unemployment has spread in an alarming way and farmers are in great distress?
It seems that the government made use of this exceptional act, to carry out, by orders in council, special measures in connection with banks, insurances, the mounted police, etc., matters which had nothing to do with the relief of unemployment and agriculture. To sum up, we can state without doubt that the government put up no valid reason to induce the house to adopt such an arbitrary measure, on the contrary, we have excellent reasons and good ground both as to the drafting and provisions of the bill, to oppose what I might call an arbitrary, vexatious, unjust and anticonstitutional measure.
I ask hon. members opposite not to forget, when voting time comes, the common hopes and trials of our forebears in the development of our country, the maintenance of self government, our political conquests, the struggles to uphold our rights which are now guaranteed by the constitution.
I trust that, in dosing my remarks, I shall be allowed to quote the following beautiful
words by Rameau:
The living image of one's country which one bears in his heart is as indestructible as the human soul itself, like the latter it revives, expands and participating to its sublime nature escapes immortal from the clasp of tyranny and subterfuges of politics.
I trust that our friends opposite are numerous who, when voting times comes, will realize as good patriots that to support such a measure is equivalent to destroying what we hold most sacred in parliament, namely the constitution, the rights and privileges which are assured and guaranteed to the representatives of the people. As in the sad days of 1926, the people, when the reckoning day comes, will certainly remember this new assault against the constitution and contempt of the liberties, attributes, privileges, rights and prerogatives of this parliament and, that day, as in 1926, the great wave of the masses will sweep everything in its path. Then shall we register again with joy, a great Liberal victory.
As it is almost six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I would ask you to be good enough to call it six o'clock.
Go on.
There are about twelve minutes yet.

Then I am very sorry that I shall have to be discourteous to the Speaker by not attending his tea. I think one of the duties of a member of parliament is to do everything in his power to uphold the dignity of the Speaker.
In making a few remarks on the resolution before the house I intend to follow my usual practice and be as brief as I possibly can. This government is plainly in trouble to-day, and you do not have to go very far, Mr. Speaker, to learn that they are in trouble, for you can read it in the expression on their faces. When did that trouble start?
You are wearing blue glasses.
When my hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Turnbull) goes back to his constituency he will need a magnifying glass to find any elector who will vote for him unless the government soon changes its policy.
You are a better politician than a prophet.

We have one member of the house that mumbles all the time; I hope that we shall not have another one. The troubles of this government started during the election campaign, and those troubles were all brought on by the government themselves, and the biggest offender in that respect was the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) himself. In 1930 he spoke at Calgary. I shall not read all that he said on that occasion because it would take up too much time, and anyway most of what he said is not worth repeating because it has not been carried out. But he did promise in that address that he would find work for every man in Canada who was willing to work. Has he done it? He knows that he has not, and his followers surrounding him know that he has not done it.
I felt truly sorry for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) when he spoke in this chamber the other day. He made the most feeble attempt I have ever known a minister of the crown to make in this house in undertaking to defend a piece of legislation. We on this side for several years listened attentively to the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce when he spoke from this side.

Unemployment Continuance Act
Then he used to make beautiful speeches, full of vim and fighting spirit, but his effort the other day was really the greatest sham I have ever witnessed.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, the troubles of this government began in the election campaign of 1930. Then, what happened in the short session of 1930 when this parliament was called together to cure unemployment? The Prime Minister asked parliament to vote him the sum of $20,000,000. That was done. What did that $20,000,000 do? It did one thing and one thing only. It did not relieve unemployment. The only thing it did do was to induce the municipalities in every part of this dominion and the provincial governments to enter upon expenditures which they otherwise would not have undertaken, so that eventually the sum of $70,000,000 was spent by the municipalities, the provincial governments, the railways and the federal government combined. But even that expenditure did nothing to relieve unemployment. Most of that money went into the pockets of contractors and of those people who control the supply of materials.
What happened next? The Prime Minister amended the tariff in order to cure unemployment, a thing which never had 'been done before in the history of this country. He put the tariff up so high that nobody could jump over it. I believe that the Prime Minister in increasing the tariff has some idea in his mind, because I observe that an order in council was passed on February 23, 1932, and reading the list of articles to which this order in council applies I am firmly convinced that he is trying to cure unemployment by preventing families from being raised. For instance, this order in council passes regulations concerning the following articles:
Baby pants: 30 cents per pound plus 40 cents per dozen.
Crib sheets: 30 cents per pound plus 35 cents per dozen.
Deflated play or water balls: 60 cents per pound.
Bathing caps: 30 cents per pound plus 30 cents per dozen.
It seems to me the Prime Minister is trying to cure unemployment by making it harder for our people to raise families. I come from a race which is well-known for its large families, and I think my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is not just to our energetic French-Canadians. Of course, a bachelor cannot appreciate the difficulties that we married men labour under. That is about all that happened, and the only thing that I can see will relieve unemployment is what I have

just stated. The Prime Minister during the campaign said he was going to "blast" his way into the markets of the world. "Listen to me, you farmers. I will make the tariffs fight for you." Well, as a commentary on that promise I have a statement here from a friend of mine. He had great hopes in this wonderful Prime Minister of ours-in fact I think a lot of people had faith in him, but they are being disillusioned. Is it not too bad the electors were fooled? In 1930, this man bought a young heifer for $20, a promising looking animal, and he took her into his herd. He is a dairyman. Last fall he thought he would get rid of her as she was not a good milker.
Was that the Prime Minister's fault too?

I am going to come to
that in a minute. My hon. friend will see by the time I am through that I am not labouring as hard as he was the other day.
I enjoyed myself.

My friend sent the
heifer to Winnipeg and it realized $4.05. He paid $3 transportation and $1 commission: his credit balance on the transaction was five cents! There is the statement, Mr. Speaker. My friend is French-Canadian, and he said to me, "Take this statement et presente le a ton moses de Bennett." Those are the exact words he used. That is how the Prime Minister has "blasted" a way into the markets of the world for the products of the farming community. This government, with its tariffs, is on the back of the agricultural industry. This government is on the back of the newborn babe-as soon as he is bom his back begins to bend with the weight of the taxation imposed by this order in council on everything he wears. That is where this government is in trouble, and it will never get out of trouble because it cannot see the light. But, thank heavens, the electorate will have a chance sooner or later to pass judgment.
Now, we are charged by our hon. friends opposite wdth delaying the supply of seed grain and other farm relief. Well, they themselves have made a fair contribution to the so-called delay. But have we really delayed this much needed relief? I find this in the regulations issued by the director of unemployment and farm relief:
All public moneys and undertakings to which contribution may be made under the provisions of clauses 6, 8, 9 and 10 of this agreement are to be carried on from the date of their commencement to the date of their completion, which latter date shall not be later than May 1, 1932.

Then if you look at another page you will find a table giving the number of provincial, municipal and federal undertakings, together with the moneys paid and the moneys still owing. But the work is going on. My hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald) in the course of his speech yesterday said:
From a fairly extensive knowledge of the operation of that arrangement, may I say that it was followed religiously.
They are very religious in the maritime provinces.
The city of Sydney, to which I referred a few moments ago, borrowed the money and spent it on public works. Those works have been passed upon and approved by the local legislature and this government. To-day however that city cannot carry on its work because this government is not in a position to pay its share.

Section 179 of the act establishes the principle that when by the closing out of a terminal or the diversion of a railway line it is made necessary, the railway board may order such compensation to employees who are forced to abandon their homes as in their judgment they deem wise. The present amendment merely extends the same principle in the event of traffic being diverted from one line to another. The added words are:
. . . nor make any change in the routing of traffic, nor run crews through divisional points where their homes are established, nor make any other change.
It also provides that thirty days' notice of the authorized change shall be given those affected. Then the amendment to section 250 merely provides that the railway commission shall have no authority to change the provision by which the standard of clearance is maintained between the top of the highest freight car and the abutments of any superstructure over the railway, until notice of the hearing has been given all parties interested. In other words, at present the board under special circumstances may deviate from the common practice and grant permission to have the clearance less than the act provides.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the amendments contained in this bill be given second reading and referred to the railway committee, where all parties can be heard.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of

Onemployment Continuance Act
Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.

Mr. Speaker, in the
twelve minutes at my disposal before six o'clock I showed that this government had been in difficulties since the election, and since the Prime Minister and his supporters broadcast their promises throughout Canada. I also showed that by the vote of $20,000,000 at the special session a combined expenditure of $70,000,000 'by the municipalities, the provinces and the railways had resulted, which otherwise would not have been made. I also proved, at least to my own satisfaction, by reading an order in council passed on the recommendation of the Minister of National Revenue, that by taxing everything required in the home the government had taken about the only method possible to relieve unemployment, and that was by preventing people from raising families because of the taxes involved.
I made reference to the fact that we have been accused of delaying the relief which might be afforded. There is a statement appearing in the Winnipeg Tribune-which is not a Liberal paper-from the Minister of Agriculture of the province of Manitoba, in answer to a question asked by a member of the legislature of that province, to the effect that seed is being provided the farmers of Manitoba, and that no delay has been occasioned. I also showed that all commitments contained in the blue book laid on the table of the house a day or two ago were being proceeded with, so there has been no delay in that regard.
After the special session of 1930, when the $20,000,000 was voted, we had the regular session of 1931, when the Prime Minister asked for a blank cheque. Mr. Speaker, I may be mistaken, but I am really, surprised to see the prime minister attempt to submit to the parliament a bill intended to substitute the word "May" for the word "March" in another law that has ceased to exist since the first instant. While not claiming to be a legal light, I think I have a certain experience of these things, I think I understand laws and I cannot help entertain the greatest doubt on the possible effect of the new law proposed by the right hon. Prime Minister. Either the law of 1931 is still effective or not; if it is, then why do they ask us to substitute in this law the word "May" for the word "March"? And I am inclined to believe that it has ceased to exist when I read paragraph 8:
This act shall expire on the first day of March, 1932.
Therefore, this act has expired; it seems to me quite evident that it has ceased to exist, if so, is it inconceivable that an act which exists no more can be amended.
The Prime Minister's tactics under these circumstances can but inspire us with the greatest distrust. How is it that previous to the expiration of the stipulated time of the 1931 act, the Prime Minister did not think of requesting parliament for an extension of the provisions of the act, which he desires to-day? What has happened to induce the Prime Minister to have recourse to this strange manoeuvre which obliges us to greatly doubt of his good intentions?
At the last session, in spite of strong protests from this side of the house, the hon. members opposite under the rod of their master forced this parliament to enact this extravagant measure, known as the "blank cheque" act.
This act is embodied in chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931 and is intituled:
An act to confer certain powers upon the Governor General in Council in respect to unemployment and farm relief, and the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada.
By this act the government conceded to themselves the power to take out of the consolidated revenue of Canada, the necessary funds and expend them as they pleased.
It goes without saying, that never, since confederation, has a government attempted to usurp such authority. If members of par-

liament have an important duty to fulfil, it is certainly, I think, that of controlling the expenditure; and the imperative duty of the government in having subsidies granted or expending the people's money, is certainly to justify, previously, where these outlays are to be made and what amounts will be required.
The 1931 act, sir, had the effect of removing this obligation and to justify himself, the Prime Minister stated then that he was unable to state the amount required to relieve unemployment and help the farmers, etc. This reason cannot be invoked to-day, and the mention of March 1, in the expired act was simply to make provision while the house would not be sitting. To-day, when parliament is assembled and the government with its past experience, is able to inform us what amounts will be required, there is not the least justification to ask for an extension of time up to May 1 for this arbitrary act of 1931. If the government could clearly prove to us that as a result of the act embodied in the statutes last year, it had succeeded to relieve the unemployed and farmers, we might trust them, and, in spite of the encroachment on the powers of parliament, we might perhaps make certain concessions and vote a stipulated amount to carry out such relief. But, sir, is it not a fact that far from having relieved the situation, unemployment has spread to an alarming extent and, that the relief given is not in proportion to the wide breach caused in our finances.
About July or August, 1931, the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Robertson) forwarded, to members and Conservative candidates defeated in the last election, a circular letter inviting us to suggest work of a federal nature that could be done in our respective counties in order to give work to the unemployed. On receipt of this letter, I immediately complied with the wishes of the hon. Minister of Labour and sent him a list of the public works that I thought were needed in the county of L'Assomption-Montcalm and, that I also considered of a nature to relieve the unemployed in the various localities. First, I mentioned what repairs were urgently required for the post office in the town of L'Assomption.
What was done to meet my suggestions? The inspector of public buildings paid a visit to L'Assomption and sent in a report that considerable repairs were needed on the post office, that the walls of the building itself were on the eve of crumbling. What was done to relieve unemployment? A carpenter
and two men were employed, for hardly five or six days, to put supports so as to prevent the walls from falling. The government should be ashamed of having the public see such a building in ruins supported by beams, when it would have been an easy task for them to rebuild the defective walls and employ during a few months the fifty or so good people who are without work and reside in the town of L'Assomption, they ask for nothing better than to work in order to support their families.
I had also pointed out to the Labour department that a public building would not be out of place at L'Epiphanie, one of the most important localities in my county where the government collects each year excise duties and postal revenue to an amount of over $50,000. I had also mentioned the necessity of building a post office in the town of St. Lin-des-Laurentides, and which had been requested for a long time past; I had also pointed out the importance of having a post office built at Ste-Julienne, the chief town of the county of Montcalm. Notwithstanding all my suggestions, the Labour department paid no attention to these public necessities which, however, were very much needed and would have given work to a large number of workmen who at present find it extremely hard to support their families.
As to agriculture, sir, I defy any member from Quebec who supports the government, and especially the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) whom I see in his seat, to mention any help whatsoever given by this government to the farmers of Quebec. Yet, all are aware of how the price of farm products have decreased in the most alarming way, notwithstanding the fine pledges of the right hon. Prime Minister during the 1930 election. Butter which then sold at 32 to 34 cents per pound sells to-day for 20 and 22 cents. The same may be said of eggs and all other farm products. Yet our opponents had publicly promised that with the advent to power of their renowned leader the greatest prosperity would reign in this country. It is thanks to these false pledges that a number of the government supporters, hailing from Quebec, were elected.
Not only did the government neglect the farming class and did not relieve the distress of these people, who are certainly the most deserving class in this country, but it did worse. By upsetting the tariff the government forced the farmer to pay much dearer for the needs of his family and to cultivate the farm, while on the other hand he is unable to sell or has to sacrifice at ridiculous prices the products of his toil.
